knowledge_point.title: Differentiating an Exponential Function with a Linear Exponent

question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $f$ as the composite function

$$
f={e}^{u},\,u=-6x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}={e}^{u},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-6.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{u}\cdot (-6) \\  & =-6{e}^{u} \\  & =-6{e}^{-6x}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y=5{e}^{4x}$ at the point where $x=\frac{1}{4}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y=5{e}^{u},\,u=4x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=5{e}^{u},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4.
$$

We now apply the chain rule and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =5{e}^{u}\cdot 4 \\  & =20{e}^{u} \\  & =20{e}^{4x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the slope of the tangent to the curve at $x=\frac{1}{4}$, we have to evaluate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{x=1/4} & ={(20{e}^{4x})|}_{x=1/4} \\  & =20{e}^{4(1/4)} \\  & =20e\end{aligned}
$$

Also, the $y$-value of the point on the curve where $x={x}_{1}=\frac{1}{4}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & ={(5{e}^{4x})|}_{x=1/4} \\  & =5{e}^{4(1/4)} \\  & =5e.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find the equation of the tangent at that point:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-5e & =20e(x-\frac{1}{4}) \\ y-5e & =20ex-5e \\ y & =20ex\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y=-3{e}^{-3x-5}-6$ at the point where $x=-2.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y=-3{e}^{u}-6,\,u=-3x-5.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=-3{e}^{u},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-3.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =-3{e}^{u}\cdot (-3) \\  & =9{e}^{u} \\  & =9{e}^{-3x-5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the slope of the tangent to the curve at $x=-2$, we have to evaluate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{x=-2} & =9{e}^{-3x-5}{|}_{x=-2} \\ & =9{e}^{(-3)(-2)-5} \\ & =9 e.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, the $y$-value of the point on the curve where $x=x_1=-2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}y_1 & =(-3{e}^{-3x-5}-6){|}_{x=-2} \\ & =-3{e}^{(-3)(-2)-5}-6 \\ & =- 3 e - 6.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find the equation of the tangent at that point:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-y_1 & =m(x-x_1) \\ y-(- 3 e - 6) & =(9 e)(x-(-2)) \\ y-(- 3 e - 6) & =9 e x-(- 18 e) \\ y & =9 e x - 6 + 15 e.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the slope $m$ of the tangent to the curve $y=-4{e}^{2-x}$ at the point where $x=2-\ln(3).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y=-4{e}^{u},\,u=2-x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=-4{e}^{u},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-1.
$$

We now apply the chain rule and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =-4{e}^{u}\cdot (-1) \\  & =4{e}^{u} \\  & =4{e}^{2-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the slope $m$ of the tangent to the curve at $x=2-\ln(3)$, we have to evaluate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point as follows

$$
\begin{aligned}m=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{x=2-\ln(3)} & =4{e}^{2-(2-\ln(3))} \\  & =4{e}^{\ln(3)} \\  & =4\cdot 3 \\  & =12.\end{aligned}
$$
